rationale: The highest-impact, lowest-risk approach is to maximize single-thread throughput without any format changes or multi-threading complexity. Fabian Giesen and dougallj have demonstrated 1.5-2x improvements over baseline zlib through careful latency analysis, multi-stream ILP, and table format optimization. Combining their techniques with sync-point discovery for virtual stream creation within standard DEFLATE blocks could yield 2x+ over zlib-ng without any thread management overhead. This is the approach most likely to be a practical drop-in replacement.
first_step: Fork libdeflate (the current fastest single-threaded DEFLATE implementation). Profile its decode loop on Skylake to identify the critical-path latency. Implement 2-way virtual stream interleaving using dougallj's sync-point algorithm. Benchmark against unmodified libdeflate on Silesia corpus.
expected_signal: If the 2-way interleaved decoder shows >15% throughput improvement over libdeflate on large blocks (>8KB), the approach is viable. If improvement is <5% or negative, the sync-point overhead is too high relative to the ILP benefit, and we should focus on larger table sizes or mega-table multi-symbol decode instead.

rationale: The fundamental tension in DEFLATE decompression is that Huffman decoding and LZ77 reconstruction are interleaved: each decoded symbol might be a literal (write directly) or a match (copy from earlier output). This interleaving prevents clean parallelization of either phase. By restructuring into two passes - first decode all Huffman symbols into a token stream (literals, lengths, distances), then execute all LZ77 copies - the Huffman pass becomes embarrassingly parallel (using sync points) while the LZ77 pass can use SIMD-accelerated copies. This trades memory (for the intermediate token buffer) for throughput.
first_step: Implement a token-buffer intermediate representation. Measure the memory overhead per block (typically 2-4 bytes per token vs 1 byte per output symbol). Profile whether the two-pass approach is faster than single-pass even without parallelizing the Huffman pass, due to better branch prediction (the Huffman loop has no literal/match branches) and better SIMD utilization (the copy loop has no Huffman decode stalls).
expected_signal: If the two-pass single-thread implementation matches or exceeds single-pass performance (even without parallel Huffman), the architecture is sound. The token buffer should be <50% of the decompressed output size. Look for >20% improvement in IPC during the Huffman-only pass compared to the interleaved decode.

rationale: For maximum throughput on multi-core systems, exploit block-level parallelism in DEFLATE streams. Most real-world DEFLATE streams contain many blocks (ZIP files may contain thousands of independently-compressed entries). Even within a single entry, DEFLATE blocks are typically 16-64KB. By speculatively finding block boundaries using heuristics (block type markers, common block sizes), multiple threads can decode different blocks in parallel. This requires the optimistic concurrency pattern: each thread decodes speculatively and validates at the end.
first_step: Analyze block-boundary patterns in real DEFLATE streams from the Silesia corpus. Implement a fast block-boundary scanner that identifies potential block starts by scanning for common dynamic Huffman header patterns. Measure the false positive rate of the scanner.
expected_signal: If block boundaries can be found with >80% accuracy using a lightweight scanner (<1% of decode time), multi-thread block parallelism is viable. For a 4-thread decoder on a 4-core machine, target 2.5-3x throughput over single-thread decode on files with >10 blocks. If false positive rate is >30%, the re-execution overhead makes this impractical.

rationale: Modern x86 CPUs have VPGATHERDD (AVX2) instructions that can perform up to 8 simultaneous 32-bit table lookups. By restructuring the Huffman decode loop to batch 8 symbol decodes and use a single gather instruction, we could achieve 8 symbols per table-access latency rather than 1. This requires careful bit-buffer management to prepare 8 independent peek values, but the potential throughput improvement is dramatic. Combined with a precomputed mega-table that encodes 2 symbols per entry, this could yield 16 symbols per gather instruction.
first_step: Benchmark VPGATHERDD latency and throughput on Skylake and Zen3. Determine if 8 independent table lookups via gather is faster than 8 sequential scalar lookups. Implement a proof-of-concept that gathers 8 table entries from a pre-positioned set of bit offsets (ignoring the serial dependency for now).
expected_signal: VPGATHERDD has high latency (~12 cycles on Skylake) but can overlap with other work. If gather-based decode achieves <1 cycle per symbol (amortized over 8 symbols), it outperforms the best scalar implementations (~2.8 cycles/byte on 3-stream Oodle). If gather latency dominates, stick with scalar multi-stream approach.
